bottom_line: Prices are still rising too fast, and the Fed (the people who set interest rates) looks almost certain to raise rates again in December. That makes borrowing more expensive, even though the economy grew faster than first reported.

stories.title: Fed set to raise rates again
stories.real: Inflation (how fast prices go up) hit 3.8%, and the Fed's favorite price gauge reached a three-year high in October. Traders now put the odds of a December rate hike at almost 100%, and the Fed looks ready to do it even though stocks have been shaky.
stories.you: Credit cards, car loans and other borrowing will likely cost more, and the Fed's final Beige Book says gas prices and interest rates are already hurting car sales.

stories.title: Trump calls GDP numbers fake
stories.real: The government sharply raised its estimate of third-quarter economic growth (GDP, the total value of everything the country produces), pointing to strong business investment and consumer spending. Trump called the revision a 'record setting error' and 'fake' and demanded an investigation of the Commerce Department.
stories.you: Strong growth plus hot inflation is the main reason the Fed thinks it can raise rates without breaking the economy.

stories.real: The White House announced new tariffs (taxes on goods brought into the U.S.) on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU. It is offering lower rates to countries that sign trade deals.
stories.you: Tariffs can push up prices on imported goods, and economists say they raise the chances that interest rates stay high for longer.

stories.title: Stocks bounce back after AI selloff
stories.real: Stocks around the world rallied as investors shrugged off the tariffs and AI worries and went looking for bargains. AI stocks bounced back after sharp losses, with Nvidia's big swings showing how risky single-stock funds can be. U.S. markets are closed for Thanksgiving.
stories.you: If you own funds that bet on one stock, like Nvidia, you're taking a much bigger and bumpier ride than you would with a broad fund.

stories.title: Poundland collapses, 11,000 jobs at risk
stories.real: UK discount chain Poundland went into administration (a kind of bankruptcy) after its owners couldn't find a buyer. Management and lawmakers blame its US owner, Gordon Brothers, which says the chain would have collapsed last year without it.
stories.you: When a big discount chain collapses, workers lose jobs and shoppers lose a cheap place to buy basics.
